Scholasticism traditionally means a highly structured method of philosophical/theological inquiry: pose a quaestio, distinguish competing positions, formulate objections, make distinctions, and arrive at a determination. Think medieval university disputation rather than free-form essay. Combat Scholasticism seems to take that argumentative machinery and turn it into a theory of intellectual conflict. The interesting word is therefore “combat.” The project appears interested in what happens when concepts aren't treated as neutral objects for contemplation but as things that operate within struggles over meaning, institutions, extraction, technology, bodies, and power. In scholastic philosophy, a formal object isn't simply “the thing we're looking at.” It's the thing considered under a particular aspect. For example, two disciplines might investigate the same physical phenomenon but have different formal objects because they're asking fundamentally different questions about it. So a “combat scholasticism” could ask: Who gets to determine what the object of thought actually is? That turns epistemology into something political and strategic. If an institution defines the object in advance, it can also constrain what questions are thinkable and what answers count as legitimate. So what does “Combat Scholasticism” actually mean? Here's my simplest formulation. Ordinary scholasticism Take a question → establish distinctions → consider objections → determine an answer. Combat Scholasticism Take a question → determine who/what controls the conditions of the question → identify what is being extracted → identify the machinery producing the conflict → identify what the machinery excludes → determine what must survive the conflict. That is why the medieval vocabulary is useful. The project isn't simply borrowing fancy Latin terminology. It's rebuilding the disputation as a diagnostic weapon. The old scholastic quaestio becomes something like a battlefield. And there's a deeper idea underneath all of it I think the strongest thread through the project is compression. Look at the recurring imagery: meaning → extraction → sealed bone → formal object → architecture → engines → shadow → planetary extension The basic problem is: When information passes through increasingly powerful systems of compression, what survives? And immediately behind that is the political question: Who gets to decide what survives? That's where Combat Scholasticism becomes much more interesting than its deliberately forbidding terminology initially suggests. Because “compression” sounds technical and neutral. But it isn't neutral. If I summarize your argument, I decide what is essential. If a platform summarizes your speech, it decides what is essential. If an AI summarizes an archive, it decides what is essential. If an institution canonizes a tradition, it decides what is essential. If history remembers one event and forgets another, something has survived compression and something has been burned. So the “sealed bone” becomes almost an epistemological survival test: After everything unnecessary has been stripped away, what must remain for this thing still to count as itself? And the “combat” is the struggle over that determination. That, to me, is the conceptual heart of the project. The archive's own documentation supports this reading especially strongly in Part I and Part II: Part I explicitly treats meaning as finite and vulnerable to extraction, while Part II asks what remains invariant when an architecture is subjected to compression.
